questions.question: What is the highest mountain in the world?
hints: It is in the Himalayas.
It sits on the border between Nepal and China.
It is almost 8,850 m (about 29,000 ft) high.
questions.description: Getting to the top takes weeks, lots of oxygen and really good socks.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's highest mountains, Pico Cristóbal Colón and Pico Simón Bolívar, are both about 5,700 m (18,700 ft) high.

questions.question: What is the fastest land animal?
hints: It's a member of the cat family.
It lives on the savannas of Africa.
It has round black spots.
questions.description: This animal never gets a speeding ticket, because nobody can catch it.
questions.fun_fact: It can run faster than 100 km/h (62 mph), but only for a few seconds.

questions.question: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
hints: It used to be found inside thermometers.
It is silvery and shiny.
It has the same name as a planet.
questions.description: A metal that never could decide between being a solid and being a smoothie.
questions.fun_fact: It is very toxic, which is why thermometers hardly use it anymore.

questions.question: What is the biggest bird in the world?
hints: It lives in Africa.
It can't fly, but it runs super fast.
It lays the biggest eggs of any bird.
questions.description: Today we're measuring birds, so we'll need a very, very tall ruler.
questions.fun_fact: An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.

questions.question: This small piece comes from a flag. Which country's flag is it?
hints: It is a country in the Americas.
Its colors are green, white and red.
It is famous for tacos and mariachis.
questions.description: A fancy lunch on top of a cactus, served right in the middle of a flag.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the Aztecs founded their great city, Tenochtitlan, right where they saw an eagle on a cactus eating a snake.

review.feedback: the flag says new mexico. so something's wrong. and either way the question doesn't wor

questions.question: Look at this close-up: which Colombian food is it?
hints: It is fried in oil until it turns golden and crispy.
Inside, it almost always has potato and meat.
It is shaped like a half moon and eaten with ají, a spicy sauce.
questions.description: An envelope that brings no letters, just something much tastier inside.
questions.fun_fact: The word “empanada” comes from the Spanish “empanar”, which means to wrap something in dough or bread.

review.feedback: this doesn't belong in the base question bundle

questions.question: What kind of tree is the tallest in the world?
hints: It grows in forests near the coast of California, in the United States.
The tallest one is taller than a 30-story building.
Its name tells you the color of its bark and wood.
questions.description: A question you'll need to tilt your head way, way back for.
questions.fun_fact: The tallest known redwood is called Hyperion, it is about 116 m (381 ft) tall, and its exact location is kept secret to protect it.

questions.question: At a store, you buy 3 empanadas at 2,500 pesos each and a soft drink for 3,000 pesos. You pay with a 20,000-peso bill. How much change do you get?
hints: First work out how much the three empanadas cost.
The three empanadas cost 7,500 pesos; now add the drink.
You spend 10,500 pesos in total: subtract that from 20,000.
questions.description: A question to find out if you can afford your snack or need to borrow money from your brother.
questions.fun_fact: Colombia's old 20,000-peso bill showed Julio Garavito, an astronomer from Bogotá who has a crater on the Moon named after him.

questions.question: Which Italian coffee dessert has a name that means “pick me up” or “cheer me up”?
hints: It is served cold, with cocoa powder dusted on top.
It is built in layers in a dish, using long sponge cookies called ladyfingers.
Its name starts with “tira”...
questions.description: A dessert with caffeine: finally, something parents and kids both want to share.
questions.fun_fact: Two Italian regions, Veneto and Friuli, have been arguing for years over which one invented tiramisu.

questions.question: In Roman numerals, what number does the letter D stand for?
hints: It's a three-digit number.
It's bigger than C, which stands for 100.
It's exactly half of M, which stands for 1,000.
questions.description: The Romans conquered half the world without a calculator, and this is how they wrote their sums.
questions.fun_fact: The Romans had no symbol at all for zero.

questions.question: An earthquake starts at a point deep underground. What is the point on the surface right above it called?
hints: This word comes up a lot in the news every time the ground shakes.
It starts with a Greek prefix that means “on” or “above.”
It literally means “the center on top.”
questions.description: When the Earth starts dancing without asking, this is where the party begins… at least when you look from above.
questions.fun_fact: The underground point where an earthquake really starts is called the hypocenter, and it can be more than 600 km (370 miles) deep.

questions.question: What is a baby sheep called?
hints: It's not the baby of a cow or a horse.
Its mom's wool is used to make scarves.
Nativity scenes often have a small, white, woolly one next to the shepherds.
questions.description: So fluffy you'd love to use it as a pillow, but it would rather you didn't.
questions.fun_fact: A sheep can recognize the faces of about 50 other sheep and remember them for years.

questions.question: Look at this picture, taken very, very close up: what is it?
hints: These little tiles are so tiny that, all together, they look like dust.
Its owner flies, but it isn't a bird.
If you touch it with your fingers, you're left with a colorful powder.
questions.description: Colorful tiles for a roof the size of a fingernail.
questions.fun_fact: The “dust” left on your fingers after touching a butterfly is thousands of tiny scales from its wings.

questions.question: What is the longest river in Africa?
hints: It crosses a huge desert before it reaches the Mediterranean Sea.
The ancient Egyptians lived along its banks.
The pyramids and the pharaohs depended on it for water and crops.
questions.description: A river so long that if you paddle it in a canoe, you'll grow a beard on the way, even if you can't grow one.
questions.fun_fact: The Nile runs about 6,650 km (4,130 miles) through 11 countries, and for thousands of years its floods made Egypt's fields fertile.

questions.question: In the rainforests of Colombia, this animal is called a saíno. It looks like a wild pig, but it isn't one. What group does it really belong to?
hints: This group lives only in the Americas, from the southern United States down to Argentina.
They look like pigs, but their family split off from pigs millions of years ago.
Scientists also call this group tayassuids.
questions.description: It has the face of a pig, the smell of cheap perfume and zero interest in being mistaken for one.
questions.fun_fact: The saíno has a gland on its back that gives off a strong smell, and the herd uses it to recognize each other.

questions.question: “Half man, half horse” is to centaur as “half woman, half fish” is to…
hints: She lives in the sea, but she is a creature from legends.
In the stories, she sings beautifully to lure sailors.
Ariel, from the Disney movie, is one of them.
questions.description: A singer who never goes on tour because she has no feet.
questions.fun_fact: When Christopher Columbus saw manatees in the Caribbean, he wrote that he had seen mermaids, but that they were not as pretty as people painted them!

questions.question: If you tie a polystyrene foam cup to an underwater robot and send it down more than 6,000 m (19,700 ft), what happens to it?
questions.answer: It shrinks into a tiny cup
wrong_answers: It bursts into a thousand bits
It puffs up like a balloon
hints: Think about all the weight of the water above the cup.
The pressure down there is hundreds of times greater than at the surface.
Polystyrene foam is full of tiny air bubbles, and the pressure squashes them.
questions.description: Down there, the water squeezes harder than a hug from Grandma.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists on deep-sea trips often decorate foam cups and send them to the bottom, and they come back as souvenirs the size of a thimble.

questions.question: I'm a saying grandmas repeat when troubles are finally over. I start like this: “After the storm comes the…”. What word do I end with?
hints: Think about how everything feels when the storm finally goes away.
It also describes a sea with no waves and no wind.
It rhymes with “palm” and means peace and quiet.
questions.description: A saying for days when everything goes wrong… until it stops going wrong.
questions.fun_fact: Many languages share this saying, and Spanish has an equally famous version: “After the storm, the sun comes out.”

questions.question: What do you call a river mouth that splits into many branches and forms a triangle, like the Nile's?
hints: The same word is also used in math and physics.
It is named after a Greek letter shaped like a triangle.
It is the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet: alpha, beta, gamma…
questions.description: A river so long that by the end it gets tired and spreads out like a fan.
questions.fun_fact: The Greek historian Herodotus called the mouth of the Nile a “delta” because it looked like the Greek letter Δ.

questions.question: In 1816, it snowed in June in Europe because of ash from Tambora, a volcano in Indonesia. Roughly how far is it from Europe?
hints: Indonesia is on the other side of the world, in Asia.
No two places on Earth are more than about 20,000 km (12,400 miles) apart.
It's roughly the distance of a flight from New York to Tokyo.
questions.description: You asked for a summer vacation and got a winter, gift-wrapped with a bow.
questions.fun_fact: People called 1816 “the year without a summer”, and the bad weather kept Mary Shelley indoors, where she wrote “Frankenstein”.

questions.question: Riddle: I'm a huge frog from North America. I was raised on farms in other countries, escaped, and now I eat the frogs there. What kind of species am I?
hints: It's a problem for the wildlife of the place where it arrived.
It's the opposite of a species native to that place.
It's like someone who walks into a stranger's house and takes over everything.
questions.description: A frog with the appetite of a bull and the manners of a guest nobody invited.
questions.fun_fact: A bullfrog will eat almost anything that fits in its mouth: insects, fish, other frogs, and even small birds!

questions.question: A harmless butterfly copies the colors of a bad-tasting one, so birds don't eat it. The trick is named after an English naturalist. What is it called?
hints: The naturalist spent eleven years collecting insects in the Amazon rainforest.
He traveled to the Amazon with Alfred Russel Wallace, but the trick isn't named after Wallace.
His first names were Henry Walter.
questions.description: Nature's most successful Halloween costume is worn all year round.
questions.fun_fact: In the Amazon, Henry Walter Bates collected about 14,700 species, and about 8,000 of them were new to science.

questions.question: Which of these cities is the capital of its country?
hints: It is a planned city, built almost from scratch.
It replaced Lagos as the capital in 1991.
It is in Nigeria.
questions.description: This influencer's GPS badly needs an update.
questions.fun_fact: Nigeria moved its capital to Abuja partly because it is closer to the center of the country than Lagos.

questions.question: Look at the photo: this Japanese sweet is the favorite food of a famous cartoon character. Whose?
hints: This character comes from the future.
It has a magic pocket full of gadgets.
It's a blue robot cat with no ears.
questions.description: Two pancakes in a tight hug, with something sweet squeezed in between.
questions.fun_fact: The filling of a dorayaki is a sweet red bean paste called “anko.”

questions.question: Complete: “Fries are to potatoes as coleslaw, the shredded salad with mayonnaise, is to…”
hints: It's a vegetable with tightly packed leaves in the shape of a ball.
The “cole” part comes from a Dutch word for this vegetable.
It's a relative of broccoli, and sauerkraut is made from it.
questions.description: A salad whose name sounds like a wizard's spell gone slightly wrong.
questions.fun_fact: “Coleslaw” comes from the Dutch “koolsla”, which means something like “cabbage salad”.

questions.question: Look at the photo: Mongolian nomads in the Gobi Desert live in this round home they can take apart and carry along. What is it called?
hints: It has a wooden frame covered with wool felt.
It isn't the cone-shaped tent of the North American plains peoples.
In Mongolian, it's called a “ger.”
questions.description: A house you can put up, take down and load onto a camel: perfect for escaping unwanted visitors.
questions.fun_fact: A Mongolian family can take down its yurt in one or two hours and load it onto just a few animals.

questions.question: It's a natural freshwater pool that forms when the roof of a cave falls in, and Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula has thousands. What is it called?
hints: The Maya used them to get water.
Many people travel to Mexico to swim in them.
The word comes from the Maya word “ts'ono'ot”.
questions.description: A natural swimming pool that made itself when the ground got tired of holding up.
questions.fun_fact: The Maya believed cenotes were doorways to Xibalba, the underworld.

questions.question: Look at this plant: it makes many cats wild with joy. Which plant family does it belong to?
hints: Look at the shape of its leaves, with edges like a saw.
Its cousins are used a lot in cooking and in herbal teas.
If you crush it, it smells a bit like a plant used in chewing gum and mojitos.
questions.description: The only plant that turns a serious cat into a 1970s hippie.
questions.fun_fact: About one in three cats feels nothing at all from catnip: whether a cat reacts to it is inherited.

questions.question: In 1947, fruit flies like this one became the first animals sent into space. Which country launched them?
hints: It wasn't the country of Laika the dog.
They used a V-2 rocket captured after the Second World War.
The launch took place in the New Mexico desert.
questions.description: Before dogs, monkeys and astronauts, space was reached by the little pest that keeps landing on your bananas.
questions.fun_fact: The flies came back alive in a capsule with a parachute, which showed that living things could survive that high up.

questions.question: Riddle me this: I live inside remote controls and toys and give them power, and when I run out, you shouldn't throw me in the regular trash. What am I?
hints: I come in many sizes: AA, AAA, square ones, and round ones as small as buttons.
When a toy stops turning on, you almost always need to change me.
I have a “+” end and a “−” end.
questions.description: Tiny, full of energy, and with a very delicate ending: just like a five-year-old cousin after a party.
questions.fun_fact: Batteries contain metals like zinc, manganese, and lithium, which can be recovered if you take them to a collection point.

questions.question: A special family dinner, hugs at midnight and presents under the tree on the night of December 24. What is this night called?
hints: It's the night just before Christmas Day.
It's not the night of December 31.
It's the night when children wait for Santa Claus to bring presents.
questions.description: The only night of the year when the whole family is awake at midnight and nobody gets scolded.
questions.fun_fact: In Spanish it's called “Nochebuena”, which means “the good night”.

questions.question: An old atlas says “Macedonia”; a new one says “North Macedonia”. In what year did the official name change?
hints: It happened only a few years ago, not in the last century.
The change came after a deal with Greece, which has a region called Macedonia.
It was just one year before the pandemic began.
questions.description: A country that added a compass direction to its name just to make peace with the neighbors.
questions.fun_fact: The fight with Greece over the name “Macedonia” lasted almost 30 years.

questions.question: “Colombia is to country as South America is to…”. Which word completes the sentence?
hints: South America is much bigger than Colombia.
Many countries fit inside South America.
Africa, Europe and Asia are one too.
questions.description: A word puzzle with more ground to cover than a family road trip.
questions.fun_fact: South America has 12 independent countries, and Brazil alone covers almost half of its land.

questions.question: I'm a pine tree in the mountains of California, over 4,800 years old. I'm named after a Bible figure famous for living 969 years. Who is he?
hints: He was the grandfather of someone famous for building an ark.
People say someone is “as old as…” him when they mean very, very old.
His name starts with M.
questions.description: A tree so old its birthday cake would need a whole forest of candles.
questions.fun_fact: The exact location of the Methuselah tree is kept secret to protect it from visitors who might want to take home a souvenir.

questions.question: The name of the Canary Islands comes from Latin and hides an animal. Which one?
hints: The Romans already knew about these islands in the Atlantic.
In Latin, this animal was called “canis.”
It's the animal that wags its tail when you come home.
questions.description: A name that looks obvious, but has hidden a surprise since Roman times.
questions.fun_fact: It's the other way around from what most people think: the canary bird is named after the islands, not the islands after the bird.

questions.question: I'm the Amazon River: in the rainy season I rise several meters and spill into the rainforest. What happens then?
wrong_answers: Pink river dolphins leave for the sea
Monkeys move down to live on the ground
hints: For months, the forest is half underwater.
Down there, visitors with fins start showing up.
Some of them eat the fruit that falls from the branches.
questions.description: A river that leaves home every year without asking permission.
questions.fun_fact: Some Amazon fish eat fruit and drop the seeds far away, so they help plant the rainforest.

questions.question: A giant tree trunk is hollowed out with fire and an ax, and left long and pointed at both ends. What is it used for?
hints: The pointed ends help it cut through something that moves.
In the rainforest, rivers are like roads.
It's going to need some paddles.
questions.description: A tree that got hollowed out and found itself a whole new career.
questions.fun_fact: Some canoes carved from a single tree trunk can carry more than ten people.

questions.question: At a school fair, one ticket buys one cupcake. In the carbon credit market, one credit stands for… what?
questions.answer: One metric ton of CO₂ kept out of the air
wrong_answers: One kilogram of CO₂ kept out of the air
One liter of CO₂ kept out of the air
100 metric tons of CO₂ kept out of the air
hints: It's an amount of greenhouse gas.
It's a fairly big unit, not one you'd use on a kitchen scale.
It's a thousand kilograms of carbon dioxide.
questions.description: Polluting with permission: the grown-up version of “I'll trade you my dessert for your homework.”
questions.fun_fact: Carbon credits became famous with the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in Japan in 1997.

questions.question: I'm a famous saint of Ireland. Legend says I taught with a three-leaf clover, and on my day, March 17, half the world wears green. Who am I?
hints: I lived more than a thousand years ago.
A huge cathedral in New York is named after me.
In Irish, my name is Pádraig.
questions.description: A saint so green that even his symbol is a plant.
questions.fun_fact: In Chicago, the city's river is dyed green to celebrate Saint Patrick's Day.

questions.question: I'm fried dough eaten at Christmas. In Mexico I'm flat and crunchy with honey; in Colombia I'm a little cheese ball. What am I?
hints: I'm fried in very hot oil.
In Spain I'm sometimes filled with cream.
My name starts with “Bu”.
questions.description: Dough, hot oil and a little patience: the recipe for happiness in December.
questions.fun_fact: Buñuelos came to the Americas with the Spanish, and each country changed them in its own way.

questions.question: Which insects ooze a yellow liquid from their legs when disturbed and are set loose in vegetable gardens to eat aphids?
hints: These insects are hunters.
Farmers use them as a natural way to control pests.
They are usually red with black spots.
questions.description: A tiny bug that drinks your plants' juice without asking first.
questions.fun_fact: Some ants look after aphids like cows, so they can drink the sweet liquid the aphids give off.

questions.question: I'm a fermented milk from the Caucasus, made with little white grains that look like tiny cauliflower. What am I?
hints: My grains are a mix of bacteria and yeasts.
I taste a little sour and a bit fizzy.
My name starts with K and ends with R.
questions.description: A milk that comes with its own little pets.
questions.fun_fact: Kefir grains grow and multiply, so you can give some away for others to make their own kefir.

questions.question: It's reddish, it comes out of a hippo's skin, and it isn't blood. Which human product does it act like?
hints: Hippos spend many hours under the African sun.
Their skin is delicate and cracks easily.
You'd put it on at the beach so you don't get burned.
questions.description: The hippo has its own beauty line, and it refuses to sell it.
questions.fun_fact: This “red sweat” also helps keep the hippo's wounds from getting infected.

questions.question: Look at this huge fossil tooth with saw-like edges. What kind of animal did it come from?
hints: Its owner lost teeth all its life and kept growing new ones.
Its owner had no bones, only cartilage.
It was a giant sea hunter with fins, and its living relatives still hunt in every ocean.
questions.description: This owner would have needed a very big toothbrush, and a whole box of spares.
questions.fun_fact: A shark can go through thousands of teeth in its life: the spare ones move forward in rows, like on a conveyor belt.

questions.question: In an official agility competition under FCI rules, the dog zigzags through the weave poles. How many poles are there?
hints: It's an even number.
It's more than 10.
It's the same as the number of months in a year.
questions.description: A dog that dodges obstacles better than you do at the mall on the first day of a big sale.
questions.fun_fact: Agility was born in England in the late 1970s, inspired by show jumping competitions for horses.

questions.question: It's French, has a white rind, is named after a region near Paris, and legend says it was crowned “king of cheeses” in 1815. Which is it?
hints: It's soft and creamy inside.
Its rind is white and velvety, not blue and not hard.
Its name is short: just four letters.
questions.description: A cheese with a crown, a white cape and the airs of French royalty.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says diplomats at the Congress of Vienna held a cheese contest, and Brie won.

questions.question: Take a close look at this tail. Which snake does it belong to?
hints: Its rings are made of keratin, just like your fingernails.
When it feels in danger, it shakes it like a maraca.
Its name includes a noisy baby toy.
questions.description: A tail that comes with its own soundtrack.
questions.fun_fact: Every time the snake sheds its skin, a new segment is added to its rattle.

questions.question: I'm Hanno, a white elephant. In 1514, I traveled from Lisbon to Rome as a gift. Who kept me as a pet?
hints: By 1514, Rome hadn't had an emperor for about a thousand years.
My owner lived in the middle of Rome and was very important to Catholics.
My owner's name was Leo X.
questions.description: Once upon a time, there was a pet so big it couldn't fit through any door.
questions.fun_fact: Hanno is said to have knelt before his owner and sprayed the crowd with water from his trunk.

questions.question: This chocolate is named after a very expensive delicacy that dogs or pigs sniff out underground. What kind of living thing is that delicacy?
hints: It grows attached to the roots of trees like the oak.
It reproduces with spores.
It's a relative of mushrooms.
questions.description: A chocolate dressed up as something pigs hunt down with their noses.
questions.fun_fact: Chocolate truffles were invented in France and got their name because they look like black truffles covered in soil.
